lines.text: "What has a living man the right to complain of?
It is his sin that each one should lament!"
But of course this glance which we turn backwards and
within, in honest self-examination, should free us to look
bravely towards the future also. Self-criticism frees us from
ever complaining about our circumstances and other people;
it gives us the calm and patient frame of mind to make an
objective judgment about men and situations, and it
renders us competent to deal with the duties which are
incumbent on us.
"How precious it is to live in patience,
and to wait quietly for the salvation of the Lord."
Have we then, in this disposition of mind, the right to hope
that our sufferings will one day come to an end, that the lot
of our nation will be changed? That once again, truthfulness
and integrity, right and justice, will come to prevail in
Germany, and that we shall be able to meet each other again
and hold intercourse in mutual trust and friendliness? That
once more we shall be able to do work that will prosper, and
have sufficient to eat? That we shall no longer have to
freeze in the bitter cold and that each will have a roof over
his head?
Yes certainly, to hope in the Lord means all this. For all
these things may we hope if we use patience and tran-
quillity—patience and calm of mind which cleanses the
mental and spiritual atmosphere, and imparts unwearied
courage and energy for action.
But it also means a great deal more! And this leads us back
to the principle that to be patient means constantly to
confess one's faith in the Lord, to decide for Him, to say:
"The Lord is my portion." This again means to choose
Him at all costs, even though the choice should entail for us
the loss of all other things. It means to make the ultimate
decision suggested by the words of the Psalmist: "Whom
have I in heaven but thee? and there is nothing upon earth
that I desire besides thee. My flesh and my heart may fail,
